broker.why: The monks examine and mark cargo; they carry no offers and arrange no terms between the lords.

custodian.quote: Each lord's soldiers held his own end
custodian.why: Guarding the road belongs to the soldiers, and the carts pass on; the monastery holds nothing in its care.

counterweight.why: Both valleys rely on the tag equally; the monastery balances no one's power against another's.

worlds.passage: For six centuries a small monastery stood at the top of the only pass between two mountain valleys, each ruled by its own lord. The lords spoke different languages and, after a long war, would let none of each other's envoys into their valleys. Monks who knew both tongues went down into each valley in turn and came back up with the other lord's latest words on grazing rights and on marriages between the two houses. The treaties that kept the peace for the next two centuries were drafted in the monastery's hall. In a history of the pass, one scholar described the monastery as, above all, the region's ______.
worlds.explanation: The lords would not meet, the monks went between them with each side's words, and the agreements were then written at the monastery, so the monastery arranged the deals: it was the region's "broker." "Checkpoint" fails because the monks themselves travel with messages and no one crossing is examined; "custodian" fails because the monastery's part is reaching agreements, not keeping anything safe; "counterweight" fails because it takes neither lord's side and brings the two together.

checkpoint.quote: went down into each valley in turn
checkpoint.why: The monks do the traveling, carrying words; the passage describes no inspection of anyone crossing.

custodian.why: The monastery's work ends in agreements between the lords, not in holding anything on someone's behalf.

counterweight.why: The monastery joins the two sides; it is not a power set against one of them.

worlds.passage: For six centuries a small monastery stood at the top of the only pass between two mountain valleys, each ruled by its own lord. When raiders burned the lowland towns, families from both valleys carried their deeds, seed grain, and church silver up to the monastery, whose walls the raiders never breached. Each family's bundle went into the vaults under a wax seal bearing its name. Families that came back down from hiding, sometimes a generation later, climbed up again and broke those seals with their own hands. In a history of the pass, one scholar described the monastery as, above all, the region's ______.
worlds.explanation: Families left their valuables sealed in the vaults, and the same families, years later, were the ones to break the seals, so the monks had held the goods untouched for them: the monastery was the region's "custodian." "Checkpoint" fails because the families climb up to leave and later reclaim goods, never to cross the pass, and nothing is examined; "broker" fails because the goods go back to their owners with no dealings between parties; "counterweight" fails because the raiders are kept out by walls, not offset by a rival power.

checkpoint.quote: climbed up again and broke those seals
checkpoint.why: The families come up to the monastery and go back down; no one passes through to the other valley or is examined.

broker.quote: under a wax seal bearing its name
broker.why: Each family's goods stay its own and come back to it; nothing is exchanged or negotiated.

counterweight.quote: whose walls the raiders never breached
counterweight.why: Safety comes from the walls around what is stored, not from a balance struck against anyone's power.

worlds.passage: For six centuries a small monastery stood at the top of the only pass between two mountain valleys, each ruled by its own lord. In time the eastern lord grew rich enough to want the western valley's pastures. The monks owned the high grazing land on the pass, chose each abbot from western families, and had the bishop's backing in every quarrel. Whenever the eastern lord gathered men to march west, the abbot gathered tenants and the bishop's letters, and for two centuries the lord never judged the march worth the cost. In a history of the pass, one scholar described the monastery as, above all, the region's ______.
worlds.explanation: Each time the eastern lord built up force, the monastery built up an answering force of its own, tenants and church backing, and the march never came, so the monastery held the balance: it was the region's "counterweight." "Checkpoint" fails because the lord is deterred by what the monastery could raise, not stopped at a gate; "broker" fails because the monastery answers one side's threat instead of arranging terms; "custodian" fails because it holds its own land and keeps nothing in trust for anyone.

checkpoint.quote: never judged the march worth the cost
checkpoint.why: The lord is held back by weighing the opposing force, not by inspection at a gate.

broker.why: The monastery answers the threat with force of its own; it negotiates nothing.

custodian.why: The land is the monastery's own; it is not keeping anyone else's property safe.

topic_tag: regional health board and an old county hospital
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: Writing about the board's first decade, one historian of medicine concluded that the board had ______ the county hospital.

worlds.passage: In 1948 a new regional health board took charge of every hospital in a rural county, among them the old stone county hospital. The board was also building a large hospital in the city forty miles away, with little money to equip it. Over the next ten years the city hospital opened its wards one at a time, and the board's records list each ward's X-ray room, operating tables, or surgeons as transferred from the county. By 1958 the stone building held only a clinic open two days a week. Writing about the board's first decade, one historian of medicine concluded that the board had ______ the county hospital.
worlds.explanation: The new hospital could not be equipped from the budget, its wards opened with machines and surgeons transferred from the county, and the county hospital ended as a part-time clinic, so the board "cannibalized" the county hospital. "Certified" fails because no standard the hospital met is described, only its emptying; "cloned" fails because the city hospital received the county hospital's own machines and surgeons rather than being built as a copy; "bartered" fails because the board moved its own property between its own hospitals and traded with no one.

certified.quote: held only a clinic open two days a week
certified.why: The hospital ends almost empty; nothing is said of its being judged against a standard.

cloned.why: The original's own equipment and staff went to the new hospital; no copy of the original was made.

bartered.quote: with little money to equip it
bartered.why: The board filled its own new building from its own older one; nothing was traded with another party.

worlds.passage: In 1948 a new regional health board took charge of every hospital in a rural county, among them the old stone county hospital. The board's records showed that patients there died after surgery less often than anywhere else in the county. Over the next ten years it opened three new hospitals in other towns. Their architects worked from drawings of the stone building, and their head nurses spent a month there before posting its staffing charts and ward rules, unchanged, in their own wards. The county hospital went on as before. Writing about the board's first decade, one historian of medicine concluded that the board had ______ the county hospital.
worlds.explanation: The board found its best hospital, then opened three more whose buildings were drawn from it and whose staffing and rules were carried over unchanged, so it "cloned" the county hospital. "Certified" fails because the board read its own records to find a model; no test the hospital had to pass is described; "bartered" fails because the hospital stayed with the board; "cannibalized" fails because nothing was taken from the original, which went on as before.

certified.why: The board uses its records to choose a model; no formal test or approval of the hospital is described.

bartered.quote: opened three new hospitals in other towns
bartered.why: The board builds hospitals itself; the county hospital is not given to anyone in exchange.

cannibalized.why: Only drawings and practices were taken; the hospital lost none of its equipment or staff.

worlds.passage: In 1948 a new regional health board took charge of every hospital in a rural county, among them the old stone county hospital. The board needed land beside its new city hospital, and the state university, which owned the plot there, had a medical school that wanted a teaching hospital in the county. In 1952 the board signed the county hospital over to the medical school, its beds, equipment, and staff included, and the board's accounts record no payment received. That same month the university's plot passed to the board. Writing about the board's first decade, one historian of medicine concluded that the board had ______ the county hospital.
worlds.explanation: Each side held what the other needed, and the whole hospital went to the medical school for no money in the same month the university's plot went to the board, so the board "bartered" the county hospital. "Certified" fails because the hospital changed hands whole, with no inspection involved; "cloned" fails because the school wanted the existing hospital and no copy was built; "cannibalized" fails because the hospital passed with its beds, equipment, and staff, so nothing was stripped out to supply the city hospital.

certified.quote: That same month the university's plot passed
certified.why: The hospital is exchanged for land; nothing judges it against a standard.

cloned.quote: wanted a teaching hospital in the county
cloned.why: The school wanted the existing hospital itself, and no copy is made anywhere.

cannibalized.quote: its beds, equipment, and staff included
cannibalized.why: The hospital leaves whole; none of its parts go to the board's other hospitals.

worlds.passage: In 1948 a new regional health board took charge of every hospital in a rural county, among them the old stone county hospital. The board had been told to enforce new national standards for wards, staff, and records, and over the next four years its inspectors visited each hospital and closed any that fell short. By 1952 the county hospital, which had kept careful records since 1890, was the only one of the county's five still open, its wards and staff unchanged. Writing about the board's first decade, one historian of medicine concluded that the board had ______ the county hospital.
worlds.explanation: The board closed every hospital that failed its inspection, and the county hospital alone was still open and unchanged afterward, so it must have passed: the board "certified" it. "Cloned" fails because the hospital survived as the single one left, not as the model for new ones; "bartered" fails because the board kept it and traded it to no one; "cannibalized" fails because its wards and staff stayed as they were.

cloned.quote: the only one of the county's five still open
cloned.why: It is the one hospital left standing as it was; no other hospital is built on its model.

bartered.why: The board's dealing with its hospitals is inspection, not an exchange with another party.

cannibalized.why: Nothing is stripped from it; it keeps everything it had.

topic_tag: a ministry's response to a river flood
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: In a later account, one reporter described the national ministry's response to the flood as ______.

worlds.passage: In 1974 a river broke through its levees and flooded some four hundred farm homes, and relief fell to the national ministry of public works. The money was ready within a week, enough to rebuild every damaged home. A family was paid once a surveyor, a district clerk, a regional office, and the ministry itself had each signed its claim, in that order, and any of them could send it back to the one before. Most families received their money the following spring. In a later account, one reporter described the national ministry's response to the flood as ______.
worlds.explanation: The money existed within a week and still took a year to arrive, because each claim had to climb four levels of sign-off in sequence, so the response was "bureaucratic." "Crude" fails because each claim was surveyed and checked, the reverse of a rough flat measure; "covert" fails because the ministry's own offices handled every claim openly; "complacent" fails because the ministry found the money at once instead of treating the flood as needing nothing.

crude.quote: once a surveyor, a district clerk
crude.why: Every claim was assessed by a surveyor and checked, which is careful, not rough or unrefined.

covert.quote: the ministry itself had each signed
covert.why: The ministry's own signature was on each payment; nothing about its role was hidden.

complacent.why: The ministry set aside full rebuilding money promptly; it did not rest on the view that nothing was needed.

worlds.passage: In 1974 a river broke through its levees and flooded some four hundred farm homes, and relief fell to the national ministry of public works. The ministry's engineers noted that the same levees had held through three higher floods in the previous forty years. On that record the minister told the district that the levees needed nothing but the gap closed, and the ministry paid to close it and for nothing more. In a later account, one reporter described the national ministry's response to the flood as ______.
worlds.explanation: Reassured by the levees' past record, the ministry treated the break as needing only a patch, so its response was "complacent." "Crude" fails because the fault is how little was done, not that what was done was rough; "covert" fails because the minister stated the decision to the district openly; "bureaucratic" fails because the decision came straight from the minister's reading of the record, with no forms, claims, or approvals involved.

crude.why: The failing is doing too little, not doing something in a rough or unrefined way.

covert.why: The decision was announced to the district directly; nothing was hidden.

bureaucratic.why: The response rests on one judgment from the levees' history, not on procedure or paperwork.

worlds.passage: In 1974 a river broke through its levees and flooded some four hundred farm homes, and relief fell to the national ministry of public works. Engineers at the ministry knew that a canal it had dug the year before had weakened the levee where it broke. That summer a church charity paid each flooded family close to what rebuilding would cost, and the ministry's statements said only that an exceptional storm had caused the break. Twelve years later, reporters found the charity's payments in the ministry's own accounts. In a later account, one reporter described the national ministry's response to the flood as ______.
worlds.explanation: The ministry knew its canal caused the break, publicly blamed a storm, and paid the families through a charity, which only its accounts revealed years later, so its response was "covert." "Crude" fails because the payments were close to each family's actual cost, not rough; "complacent" fails because the ministry knew it was at fault and paid for it; "bureaucratic" fails because the charity paid the families directly, with no procedure to work through.

crude.quote: close to what rebuilding would cost
crude.why: Payments were matched to the cost of rebuilding, which is the opposite of rough or one-size.

complacent.why: The ministry knew its own work caused the break and acted on it; it was not resting on a good record.

bureaucratic.quote: a church charity paid each flooded family
bureaucratic.why: The money reached families straight from the charity; no official procedure stood in the way.

worlds.passage: In 1974 a river broke through its levees and flooded some four hundred farm homes, and relief fell to the national ministry of public works. The ministry acted within a day. Its trucks drove through the district handing a check for one fixed sum to whoever came to the door, without taking names, and tipped sandbags out unfilled at the roadside. A family whose cellar had taken a foot of water got what a family whose house had washed away got, and many sandbags washed away, unstacked, in the next storm. In a later account, one reporter described the national ministry's response to the flood as ______.
worlds.explanation: The ministry moved fast and openly, but with no measurement at all: one sum handed to anyone at the door whatever the loss, and sandbags dumped unfilled, so the response was "crude." "Covert" fails because the ministry's trucks delivered the aid in the open; "complacent" fails because it acted within a day; "bureaucratic" fails because there were no claims, no records, not even names: the opposite of procedure.

covert.quote: Its trucks drove through the district
covert.why: The aid came openly from the ministry's own trucks; nothing about its source was hidden.

complacent.why: An immediate response rules out a ministry satisfied that nothing needed doing.

bureaucratic.quote: to whoever came to the door, without taking names
bureaucratic.why: Money went out with no claim, record, or check of any kind, so no procedure governed it.

topic_tag: a chemist and his laboratory technician
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: One biographer has described the technician as, more than anything, the chemist's ______.

worlds.passage: From 1951 to 1966 a chemist at a small university laboratory worked with a single technician, a young woman who had answered his newspaper advertisement. For her first year she only washed glassware. After that the chemist had her carry out the steps of his syntheses at his bench while he stood beside her, adding a few more steps each month. When he retired in 1966, the university gave his laboratory to her, and the syntheses in her own later papers follow his down to the order in which the flasks are washed. One biographer has described the technician as, more than anything, the chemist's ______.
worlds.explanation: She moved from washing glass to doing his syntheses step by step under his eye, then inherited his laboratory and kept his methods exactly, so she was the chemist's "apprentice." "Audience" fails because she learned by doing the work, not by listening; "ambassador" fails because everything she does is inside the laboratory, and she represents him to no one; "accomplice" fails because what she carries on is his method, openly, not any wrongdoing.

audience.quote: carry out the steps of his syntheses
audience.why: She performs the work herself; she is not there to listen while he explains.

ambassador.why: Her path runs from learning his bench work to inheriting it; she speaks for him to no one outside.

accomplice.quote: follow his down to the order
accomplice.why: What she takes from him is his craft, carried on openly in her own papers, not a part in wrongdoing.

worlds.passage: From 1951 to 1966 a chemist at a small university laboratory worked with a single technician, a young woman who had answered his newspaper advertisement. She never touched the apparatus and understood little chemistry. Each evening the chemist described the day's experiments aloud to her as she typed his notes, often stopping mid-sentence to cross out a plan, and he said that only when he explained a step to someone could he see where it would fail. One biographer has described the technician as, more than anything, the chemist's ______.
worlds.explanation: Her role was to be someone the chemist could talk to: explaining his plans aloud to her let him find their flaws, though she followed little of it, so she was the chemist's "audience." "Apprentice" fails because she never did the work and never learned the science; "ambassador" fails because she spoke for him to no one; "accomplice" fails because nothing wrong is being done, only his own thinking clarified.

apprentice.why: She never practiced the craft and never learned it, so she was not being trained to do his work.

ambassador.quote: described the day's experiments aloud to her
ambassador.why: The talk runs from him to her inside the laboratory; she carries none of it to anyone else.

accomplice.why: The purpose is honest self-correction of his plans, with no wrongdoing to take part in.

worlds.passage: From 1951 to 1966 a chemist at a small university laboratory worked with a single technician, a young woman who had answered his newspaper advertisement. In 1964 he published yields that no other laboratory could reproduce, and the agency that funded him announced that its inspectors would examine his notebooks and samples. The week before they came, she worked late every night at his request. The notebooks the inspectors read were in her handwriting throughout, and the sample shelves stood empty. One biographer has described the technician as, more than anything, the chemist's ______.
worlds.explanation: His results could not be reproduced and inspectors were coming; in the week before, she worked nights at his request, and the inspectors found notebooks rewritten in her hand and no samples to test, so she helped him cover up: she was the chemist's "accomplice." "Audience" fails because she acted rather than listened; "apprentice" fails because nothing is taught or learned, only records remade; "ambassador" fails because she prepares to keep his work from outsiders rather than presenting it to them.

audience.quote: worked late every night at his request
audience.why: Her part is active work for him, not listening to him.

apprentice.why: She remakes his records; she is not being trained in his craft.

ambassador.why: Facing outsiders, the laboratory hides its work from examination rather than presenting it.

worlds.passage: From 1951 to 1966 a chemist at a small university laboratory worked with a single technician, a young woman who had answered his newspaper advertisement. The chemist disliked travel, never once attended a meeting, and answered letters from other scientists only through her. Each spring she spent a month at laboratories across the country, and the sample exchanges and joint papers of those years were all settled during her visits. One biographer has described the technician as, more than anything, the chemist's ______.
worlds.explanation: He would not travel, meet, or write to other scientists himself, and every agreement with other laboratories was settled on her visits, so she represented him: she was the chemist's "ambassador." "Audience" fails because she deals with others for him rather than listening to him; "apprentice" fails because nothing describes her learning his work, only settling his dealings; "accomplice" fails because the dealings with other laboratories are open, with nothing wrong concealed.

audience.quote: spent a month at laboratories across the country
audience.why: She is out among other scientists, not listening to the chemist.

apprentice.why: What she handles is his dealings with other laboratories, not training in his craft.

accomplice.why: His work goes openly to other scientists through her; there is no wrongdoing to share in.

topic_tag: a coastal trading house and a river town's grain trade
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: One economic historian has argued that by 1800 the house had ______ the town's grain trade.

worlds.passage: In 1782 a trading house from the coast opened an office in a river town where farmers from the surrounding district had long sold their grain. Over the next decade it bought the harvest of nearly every farm in the district at the town's scales and leased both of the town's warehouses. By the late 1790s harvests were as large as ever, the millers downriver were paying more for the town's grain each autumn, and each year's price matched the figure the house's agent posted on the market door. One economic historian has argued that by 1800 the house had ______ the town's grain trade.
worlds.explanation: The house bought nearly all the grain and all the storage, and afterward the price rose with steady harvests to whatever its agent posted, so it controlled supply and price: it "cornered" the town's grain trade. "Awakened" fails because farmers had long sold grain in the town; "bankrolled" fails because the house bought the grain itself rather than funding others; "coordinated" fails because, holding the harvest and both warehouses, it took the trade over rather than organizing other dealers.

awakened.why: The trade was already active when the house came, so there was nothing dormant to revive.

bankrolled.quote: bought the harvest of nearly every farm
bankrolled.why: The house did the buying itself; it was not lending to others who traded.

coordinated.quote: leased both of the town's warehouses
coordinated.why: The house held the grain and the storage itself, leaving no separate dealers whose activity it organized.

worlds.passage: In 1782 a trading house from the coast opened an office in a river town where farmers from the surrounding district had long sold their grain. The house never bought or sold a sack of grain itself. Each spring the forty small dealers who bought from the farmers signed notes at its office, and each autumn, once the millers had paid them, they came back to settle those notes with interest. In 1794, when the house shut its office for one season, half of the dealers bought no harvest at all. One economic historian has argued that by 1800 the house had ______ the town's grain trade.
worlds.explanation: The dealers signed notes each spring and repaid them with interest after selling, and when the house closed for a season half of them could not buy, so the trade ran on the house's money: it "bankrolled" the town's grain trade. "Cornered" fails because the house held no grain; "awakened" fails because farmers had long sold grain there; "coordinated" fails because each dealer's tie to the house was his own debt, not a shared arrangement among the dealers.

cornered.quote: never bought or sold a sack
cornered.why: The house held no grain at all, so it could not control the supply.

awakened.why: The trade was already going when the house arrived.

coordinated.why: Each dealer dealt with the house separately over money; nothing organizes the dealers' activity together.

worlds.passage: In 1782 a trading house from the coast opened an office in a river town where farmers from the surrounding district had long sold their grain. At the house's urging, the forty small dealers who bought from the farmers agreed to bring grain to market on set days in turn and to store it in one shared warehouse. Each month their barges went downriver together in a single convoy, on a timetable that the house drew up and posted for a small fee. One economic historian has argued that by 1800 the house had ______ the town's grain trade.
worlds.explanation: The dealers kept trading but fitted their market days, storage, and shipping to one plan the house urged and timetabled, so it "coordinated" the town's grain trade. "Cornered" fails because the forty dealers still did the buying; "awakened" fails because the trade was long established; "bankrolled" fails because money flowed to the house as a fee for the timetable, not from it to the dealers.

cornered.quote: the forty small dealers who bought from the farmers
cornered.why: The buying stayed in forty hands, so the house controlled no supply.

awakened.why: The trade was already active; nothing was revived.

bankrolled.why: The dealers paid the house for a timetable; the house supplied no funds to them.

worlds.passage: In 1782 a trading house from the coast opened an office in a river town where farmers from the surrounding district had sold their grain until the 1740s. The river had then silted up, the millers downriver had turned to other towns, and the market square had stood empty for forty years. The house dredged the channel, sent one barge of grain downriver that autumn, and closed its office the next spring, and within a decade thirty local dealers were shipping grain from the town again. One economic historian has argued that by 1800 the house had ______ the town's grain trade.
worlds.explanation: A trade that had lain dead for forty years came back to life after the house reopened the river and sent one cargo, so it "awakened" the town's grain trade. "Cornered" fails because the house left after one season and thirty local dealers took up the trade; "bankrolled" fails because the house cleared the channel rather than funding the dealers; "coordinated" fails because it was gone before the dealers returned, so it organized none of them.

cornered.quote: closed its office the next spring
cornered.why: The house left the trade almost at once; it never controlled the supply.

bankrolled.why: Its contribution was reopening the river, not lending to the dealers who later traded.

coordinated.quote: within a decade thirty local dealers
coordinated.why: The dealers returned after the house had gone, so it arranged nothing among them.

topic_tag: a city's new central library building
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: Reviewing it that year, one critic called the building, above all, ______.

worlds.passage: In 1968 a city opened a new central library, designed by a young architect, on the site of an old train station. The city council had asked for murals in the lobby, carved oak doors, and a carpeted reading room. The architect, who said that a library should hold nothing to draw the eye from the page, built none of them, and he left the gray concrete of the outer walls unpainted inside the low reading rooms as well. Reviewing it that year, one critic called the building, above all, ______.
worlds.explanation: Every ornament the council asked for was left out on principle, and even the bare outer concrete was carried inside, so the building was "austere." "Airy" fails because its reading rooms are low and concrete-walled, not spacious and light; "adaptable" fails because the design choice is omission of ornament, not a layout that can be changed; "accessible" fails because the architect's aim concerns what the eye meets, not how readers get in.

airy.why: The rooms are low and walled in bare concrete, not open and full of light.

adaptable.why: The design is defined by what was left out, not by a space that can be rearranged.

accessible.quote: nothing to draw the eye from the page
accessible.why: The governing idea is plainness for the reader's attention, not ease of entry or use.

worlds.passage: In 1968 a city opened a new central library, designed by a young architect, on the site of an old train station. The old library had stood at the top of forty steps on a hill, and its readers had filled out slips for clerks to fetch books from closed stacks. The new one stood beside the bus terminal, and in its first month more children and wheelchair users came through its doors than the old library had seen in a year, most of them heading straight for the shelves of the reading rooms. Reviewing it that year, one critic called the building, above all, ______.
worlds.explanation: Set against an old library up forty steps with closed stacks, the new one drew more children and wheelchair users in a month than the old one saw in a year, straight to shelves they could reach themselves, so it was "accessible." "Airy" fails because nothing describes its space or light, only who could get in; "austere" fails because nothing describes bare or plain interiors; "adaptable" fails because the comparison concerns reaching books, not changing the rooms.

airy.why: The building is described by where it stands and who comes in, not by spacious or light-filled rooms.

austere.why: What is new is that readers reach the books themselves, not plainness of decoration.

adaptable.quote: top of forty steps on a hill
adaptable.why: The contrast with the old library is about difficulty of reaching books, not flexibility of the space.

worlds.passage: In 1968 a city opened a new central library, designed by a young architect, on the site of an old train station. In its first year the room that had opened as a music library became a children's library by spring and an exhibition hall by autumn. Each change took the staff a single weekend, and neither needed builders, new walls, or the closing of any other part of the building. Reviewing it that year, one critic called the building, above all, ______.
worlds.explanation: One room took on two new uses within a year, each time in a weekend and with no construction at all, so the building was "adaptable." "Airy" fails because nothing describes the rooms' height or light, only their changing use; "austere" fails because nothing is said about plain or bare decoration; "accessible" fails because the changes concern what the room is for, not how readers get in.

airy.why: The passage describes changes of use, not space or daylight.

austere.quote: Each change took the staff a single weekend
austere.why: The building's quality is how quickly it can be remade, not plainness of finish.

accessible.why: The point is ease of changing the space, not ease of entry for readers.

worlds.passage: In 1968 a city opened a new central library, designed by a young architect, on the site of an old train station. The architect placed the main reading room on the top floor, under a ceiling three stories high, with tiled murals on its walls and potted trees between the tables. On most days the staff switched on no lamps there at all, since the whole roof was made of glass panels. Reviewing it that year, one critic called the building, above all, ______.
worlds.explanation: A room three stories tall, roofed in glass so that daylight alone lit it, is spacious and full of light: the building was "airy." "Austere" fails because the room has tiled murals and potted trees, not bare surfaces; "adaptable" fails because nothing about the room can be moved or changed; "accessible" fails because the main room sits on the top floor and nothing is said of ease of entry.

austere.why: The room is decorated, not stripped bare.

adaptable.quote: under a ceiling three stories high
adaptable.why: The room's quality is its fixed height and glass roof, not a layout that changes.

accessible.quote: main reading room on the top floor
accessible.why: Placing the main room at the top works against easy entry; the design is about light and space.

topic_tag: a rural poet and her brother in the city
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: Her biographer describes the brother, in the end, as the poet's ______.

worlds.passage: For forty years a poet lived on her family's farm, two days' ride from the city where her younger brother lived and where her books were printed. When the farm failed in 1880, he paid off its debts. From then on a draft on his bank reached the farm on the first of every month, and she gave up the village teaching that had left her no hours to write. Nearly all of her published poems date from after 1880. Her biographer describes the brother, in the end, as the poet's ______.
worlds.explanation: He cleared the farm's debts, then sent money monthly, which let her quit the teaching that had kept her from writing, and the poems followed, so he was the poet's "benefactor." "Critic" fails because his effect on the poems runs through her freed time, and nothing says he judged them; "courier" fails because what travels is his money to her, not her poems to the city; "confidant" fails because the tie described is financial support, with no private matters shared.

critic.why: His effect on her poetry is through giving her time to write, not through judging what she wrote.

courier.quote: a draft on his bank reached the farm
courier.why: What moves between them is his money to her, not her poems to the printer.

In the symphony the violins play it note for note from start to finish while the cellos play the village's wedding song at the same time. Each tune's high notes fall where the other's low notes are, so that a listener can follow either one the whole way through. Comparing the symphony with the village version, one critic observed that the composer had ______ the tune.
worlds.explanation: A tune once played alone now runs together with a second tune, the two fitted so each stays clear against the other, so the composer "braided" the tune. "Clipped" fails because it is played from start to finish; "animated" fails because the change is a second line joined to it, not a livelier pace; "cleansed" fails because it is kept note for note.

clipped.why: The whole tune is played, so none of it is cut off.

animated.why: The change is the fitting of a second melody to it, not a quicker or livelier rhythm.

cleansed.why: The tune's own notes are untouched, so nothing in it was removed as rough.

worlds.passage: In 1907 a composer built one movement of his first symphony on a folk tune he had heard in a fishing village. In the symphony the orchestra plays the phrase the children knew, note for note and at the fiddlers' own speed, over and over until the movement ends. Comparing the symphony with the village version, one critic observed that the composer had ______ the tune.

animated.why: Its pace is unchanged, so it was not made livelier.

cleansed.why: What remains is exactly the village notes; the change is in length only.

In an oral history recorded decades later, one fellow trustee called her the board's ______ during those years.
worlds.explanation: Only her committee could put spending on the agenda, and only about five of forty requests a year got past it to a board that approved almost all it saw, so she controlled what reached the board: its "gatekeeper." "Figurehead" fails because that control was real power, not a title without it. "Envoy" fails because her work was screening requests coming in, not representing the board to anyone outside it. "Holdout" fails because she was not resisting a decision the other trustees had reached.

worlds.passage: For most of the 1960s a retired surgeon sat on the nine-member board of trustees of a county hospital. worlds.passage: For most of the 1960s a retired surgeon sat on the nine-member board of trustees of a county hospital. worlds.explanation: The board joined by eight to one and renewed every year, and she alone kept voting no for five years while every other board in the county agreed, so she was the board's "holdout." "Gatekeeper" fails because her votes controlled nothing: the hospital joined and renewed regardless. "Figurehead" fails because she acted on her own judgment rather than lending a name to others' decisions. "Envoy" fails because she opposed the board's majority rather than representing it to outsiders.

topic_tag: a harvest procession over fifty years

As those families sold their groves and moved to the coast, the village councils stopped asking whose son a singer was, and by the 1980s most of those who carried the lanterns were hired pickers and their daughters. Writing in 1990, one folklorist concluded that the changes of the previous fifty years had ______ the custom.
worlds.explanation: Roles once inherited by six families' sons stopped being checked for lineage, and hired pickers and their daughters came to fill them, so the changes had "democratized" the custom. "Dramatized" fails because nothing turned the procession into a show for an audience; only who took part changed. "Enshrined" fails because no law or formal honor fixed it in place; the councils loosened its rules. "Harmonized" fails because the change concerned who performed, not differences among the villages' versions.

topic_tag: enforcing a street-vending ordinance

worlds.passage: In 2015 a city passed an ordinance limiting where street vendors could park their carts. The city's four inspectors checked carts in whatever neighborhood their other work, mostly restaurant and building inspections, took them to on a given day. A review of the first year's tickets found that three blocks near the city's permit office, where that other work often took them, accounted for half of all fines, while carts parked the same way in other neighborhoods went months without a visit. Asked about its first year, most of the vendors interviewed for one study described the city's enforcement of the ordinance as ______.
worlds.explanation: Inspectors checked carts only where unrelated work happened to take them, so fines piled up on a few blocks while identical carts elsewhere went unvisited: the enforcement was "haphazard," following no plan of its own. "Evenhanded" fails because vendors doing the same thing were treated very differently depending on location. "Furtive" fails because nothing suggests the inspectors concealed their checks. "Drastic" fails because the passage describes how unevenly enforcement fell, not how severe its penalties were.

evenhanded.quote: carts parked the same way in other neighborhoods went months without a visit
evenhanded.why: identical conduct drew fines in one place and nothing in another, so treatment was unequal

furtive.why: inspections followed the inspectors' other errands, a matter of chance, not concealment

drastic.quote: accounted for half of all fines
drastic.why: the pattern described concerns where fines fell, not the severity of the penalties

worlds.passage: In 2015 a city passed an ordinance limiting where street vendors could park their carts. Inspectors were told to work in their own clothes, to buy a snack or a drink at each cart they checked, and to say nothing about the ordinance while they were there. Weeks later a vendor might receive a fine by mail naming a date and a corner, and many could not recall which of that day's buyers had been the inspector. Asked about its first year, most of the vendors interviewed for one study described the city's enforcement of the ordinance as ______.
worlds.explanation: Inspectors were instructed to blend in as buyers and keep quiet, and vendors learned of a check only weeks later by mail, unable to say who had made it, so the enforcement was "furtive," carried out by stealth. "Haphazard" fails because the inspectors followed deliberate instructions. "Evenhanded" fails because nothing indicates vendors were treated alike; the point is that they could not see the enforcement. "Drastic" fails because the penalty described is an ordinary mailed fine.

haphazard.quote: Inspectors were told to work in their own clothes
haphazard.why: the method was a set instruction, not the absence of a plan

evenhanded.quote: could not recall which of that day's buyers
evenhanded.why: what vendors report is that the checks were invisible to them, not that they were treated equally

drastic.why: the penalty is an ordinary fine; the striking feature is secrecy, not severity

worlds.passage: In 2015 a city passed an ordinance limiting where street vendors could park their carts. The city's inspectors worked monthly through a list of licensed carts ordered by license number, and a vendor found in a restricted zone got a written warning and, on a second offense, a fine. On that list a lone owner's stall might follow a truck from the city's largest fleet, and in the first year those trucks made up a fifth of the city's carts and a fifth of its fines. Asked about its first year, most of the vendors interviewed for one study described the city's enforcement of the ordinance as ______.

"Haphazard" fails because the inspectors followed a fixed list on a monthly cycle. "Furtive" fails because a written warning before any fine is open, not stealthy. "Drastic" fails because a first offense brought only a warning.

haphazard.quote: worked monthly through a list of licensed carts
haphazard.why: a fixed list on a monthly cycle is systematic, not random

furtive.why: vendors were told openly before any penalty, so the enforcement was not secret

drastic.quote: on a second offense, a fine

worlds.passage: In 2015 a city passed an ordinance limiting where street vendors could park their carts. Under the earlier rules, an inspector who found a cart in the wrong place had simply asked its owner to move along. "Evenhanded" fails because the passage measures how severe the response became, and it left the penalty to each inspector's choice rather than to one standard.

haphazard.quote: chose towing in nine of every ten cases
haphazard.why: a near-uniform choice of the harshest option is a consistent pattern, not chance

furtive.quote: holding each cart for thirty days
furtive.why: impounding carts is open and visible, the reverse of secret

topic_tag: an outbreak in a stand of oaks
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: Summing up three decades of surveys, one forester wrote that the outbreak had ______ the oaks.

worlds.passage: Since 1985 foresters have surveyed a stand of oaks on a dry ridge every summer, and in the early 1990s an outbreak struck it. The outbreak was a root fungus, which rots the thick roots that anchor an oak while its trunk stays sound and its crown stays in full leaf. As the rot spread, the surveys measured the oaks leaning a little further each year. By 2005 they recorded open ground where the stand had been, with the trunks lying across it, each still attached to a rotted mass of roots. Summing up three decades of surveys, one forester wrote that the outbreak had ______ the oaks.
worlds.explanation: The fungus rotted only the anchoring roots, so the full-grown trees leaned further each year until they lay on the ground, roots rotted through: the outbreak had "felled" the oaks. "Dwarfed" fails because the trees were full-size, with sound trunks and full crowns, when they came down. "Defoliated" fails because the fungus attacked roots and left the crowns in leaf. "Honeycombed" fails because the trunks stayed sound; the damage was below ground.

defoliated.quote: its crown stays in full leaf
defoliated.why: the fungus worked only on the roots, so the leaves were not stripped

honeycombed.why: the wood of the trunk was untouched; only the roots rotted

worlds.passage: Since 1985 foresters have surveyed a stand of oaks on a dry ridge every summer, and in the early 1990s an outbreak struck it. The stand had been replanted after a fire in 1988, and the outbreak was a mildew that killed the growing tip of each young oak's main stem every spring. Each tree sent out side branches below the dead tip, and by 2019 the surveys measured the oaks at about the height they had reached in 1993, while same-age oaks on an untouched ridge nearby had reached twenty feet. Summing up three decades of surveys, one forester wrote that the outbreak had ______ the oaks.

"Felled" fails because the trees were alive and branching. "Defoliated" fails because the mildew killed only the growing tip. "Honeycombed" fails because nothing bored into the wood; the harm was to upward growth.

felled.why: trees still putting out branches are alive and standing

defoliated.why: the mildew destroyed the stem's tip, not the leaves

honeycombed.why: the attack was on new shoots at the tip, not on the wood inside

worlds.passage: Since 1985 foresters have surveyed a stand of oaks on a dry ridge every summer, and in the early 1990s an outbreak struck it. The outbreak was a moth whose caterpillars hatch in spring and feed on oak leaves until midsummer. For three straight years they were so numerous that, by July, photographs taken from a plane showed the ground beneath the stand as plainly as in winter, and each spring the oaks put out new growth that the next generation of caterpillars consumed in turn. Summing up three decades of surveys, one forester wrote that the outbreak had ______ the oaks.

"Honeycombed" fails because the caterpillars fed on leaves, not wood.

felled.quote: each spring the oaks put out new growth
felled.why: trees that grow again every spring are alive and standing

dwarfed.why: a canopy over the ground means grown trees, not stunted ones

honeycombed.why: the damage was to the foliage; nothing tunneled into the wood

worlds.passage: Since 1985 foresters have surveyed a stand of oaks on a dry ridge every summer, and in the early 1990s an outbreak struck it. The outbreak was a beetle whose larvae bore into the heartwood of mature oaks, each one feeding for several years along a path of its own before it emerges. Through the 2000s the surveys measured every tree with a full crown, and cores drilled from a dozen of the oaks in 2016 came up in short pieces, broken every few inches along their whole length. Summing up three decades of surveys, one forester wrote that the outbreak had ______ the oaks.
worlds.explanation: Each larva tunneled its own path through the heartwood for years, and cores broke apart every few inches along their length, so the trunks were riddled with passages: the outbreak had "honeycombed" the oaks. "Felled" fails because surveys kept recording the trees' full crowns. "Dwarfed" fails because the beetle attacked mature trees, not young ones held small. "Defoliated" fails because the crowns stayed full; the damage was hidden inside the wood.

felled.quote: the surveys measured every tree with a full crown
felled.why: trees whose crowns are surveyed every summer are still standing

dwarfed.why: the trees attacked were already grown, so their size was not stunted

defoliated.why: the beetle fed inside the wood, not on leaves

Looking back, one historian called the pamphlet the movement's ______ in its first decade.
worlds.explanation: Branches opened the pamphlet to the relevant chapter as each item of business arose and kept its procedures current, so it served as the movement's "handbook," a practical guide in daily use. "Gospel" fails because a pamphlet repeating commonplace arguments, left unread, was not the movement's revered authority. worlds.passage: In the spring of 1936 a flood swept the length of a narrow farming valley, where a river had run for centuries between orchards and cornfields to a rocky gorge at the valley's lower end. Its waters tore loose thousands of logs from a lumber camp upstream and carried them, with boulders from the banks, into that gorge, where they wedged between the rock walls. For nine years afterward the lower fields lay under still water that stood higher every spring, until engineers blasted a channel through the gorge in 1945. Revisiting the valley a decade later, one geographer wrote that the flood had ______ it.
worlds.explanation: Logs and boulders wedged in the gorge at the valley's outlet, still water stood over the fields and rose each spring, and it took blasting to open a channel, so the flood had "dammed" the valley. "Gouged" fails because the flood plugged the outlet and held water rather than cutting into the floor. "Emptied" fails because the valley filled with water instead of losing its contents. "Flattened" fails because the effect described is blocked, standing water, not growth laid flat.

gouged.quote: where they wedged between the rock walls
gouged.why: the flood deposited debris that blocked the outlet; it did not cut into the ground

emptied.quote: lay under still water that stood higher
emptied.why: the valley filled up rather than being emptied

flattened.why: the lasting problem was a blockage that had to be opened, not crops or trees knocked down

worlds.passage: In the spring of 1936 a flood swept the length of a narrow farming valley, where a river had run for centuries between orchards and cornfields to a rocky gorge at the valley's lower end. Swollen by snowmelt, the river left its winding bed for a straight course down the valley floor, and for eleven days fast water ran through the soft soil. Farmers returning to their fields found the river running in a channel twenty feet below them, and bridges were needed where wagons had once crossed level ground. Revisiting the valley a decade later, one geographer wrote that the flood had ______ it.
worlds.explanation: Eleven days of fast water through soft soil left the river at the bottom of a twenty-foot channel that had to be bridged, so the flood had "gouged" the valley. "Dammed" fails because the river kept flowing along its new course. "Emptied" fails because the change was a deep cut in the land, and the farmers came back to their fields. "Flattened" fails because the flood carved a deep channel instead of laying anything level.

dammed.quote: a straight course down the valley floor
dammed.why: the water ran freely down a new course, so nothing held it back

emptied.why: the farmers came back, so the valley was not emptied of its people

flattened.quote: bridges were needed where wagons had once crossed
flattened.why: the ground once level now needed bridging, the reverse of being laid flat

worlds.passage: In the spring of 1936 a flood swept the length of a narrow farming valley, where a river had run for centuries between orchards and cornfields to a rocky gorge at the valley's lower end. The water rose slowly and lay on the fields for six weeks, and when it drained it left behind a crust of salt carried up from the coastal marshes. Nothing planted in the next three springs would grow, and by 1946 the valley's school, which had needed four teachers before the flood, had closed for lack of pupils. Revisiting the valley a decade later, one geographer wrote that the flood had ______ it.
worlds.explanation: Salt left by the water ruined the fields for years, and the school that had needed four teachers closed for want of children, so the flood had "emptied" the valley of its families. "Dammed" fails because the water drained away after six weeks. "Gouged" fails because the water left a crust on the land rather than cutting into it. "Flattened" fails because slowly rising water knocks nothing over; the harm came from the salt.

dammed.why: the water ran off after six weeks, so nothing held it back

gouged.quote: left behind a crust of salt
gouged.why: the flood deposited salt on the surface rather than cutting channels

flattened.why: slowly rising water does not push things over; the damage came from what it left

worlds.passage: In the spring of 1936 a flood swept the length of a narrow farming valley, where a river had run for centuries between orchards and cornfields to a rocky gorge at the valley's lower end. Driven by a gale, a wall of water a few feet high crossed the valley in less than an hour and was gone by evening. Surveyors later found every orchard tree and cornstalk still rooted in soil the water had barely disturbed, and photographs from the ridge show the valley floor striped in the direction the water had run. Revisiting the valley a decade later, one geographer wrote that the flood had ______ it.
worlds.explanation: A fast, shallow wall of water left trees and stalks rooted in undisturbed soil yet showed from above as stripes running with the current, so it had laid them over: the flood had "flattened" the valley's growth. "Dammed" fails because the water was gone within hours. "Gouged" fails because the soil was barely disturbed. "Emptied" fails because the trees and crops stayed rooted where they grew.

emptied.why: the crops and trees stayed in place, so the valley was not emptied

topic_tag: the prose of a farmer's memoir
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: Critics who reviewed the book found its prose ______ from first chapter to last.

worlds.passage: In 1958 a retired wheat farmer published a memoir of his forty years on the plains, with a chapter for each season of the farm year. Each chapter recounts that season's work, a dry summer or a hard winter, and its last pages turn to "the young man starting out," whom the author addresses directly throughout the book. A chapter about a runaway mule ends like all the others, with three rules for that young man about fences and debt drawn from the mule's escape. Critics who reviewed the book found its prose ______ from first chapter to last.
worlds.explanation: Every chapter, even one about a runaway mule, closes by turning to a young reader and handing him rules drawn from the episode, so the prose is "didactic," written to instruct. "Deadpan" fails because the author does not report events and leave them; he draws rules from each one. "Digressive" fails because each chapter goes from its season's work straight to its rules. "Florid" fails because the prose is marked by its lessons, not by ornate language.

deadpan.quote: three rules for that young man
deadpan.why: an author who extracts rules from each episode is commenting on it, not reporting it flatly

digressive.why: every chapter keeps one fixed course from its season to its lesson, so it does not wander

florid.why: the distinctive feature is direct instruction of the reader, not elaborate figures of speech

worlds.passage: In 1958 a retired wheat farmer published a memoir of his forty years on the plains, with a chapter for each season of the farm year. In the chapter on one hard winter he reports a barn fire, a hailstorm that killed his only cow, and a banker who fled with his savings, each in the tone he uses elsewhere for the price of seed. Readers laughed hardest at details he passed over as quickly as the rest, such as the cow's having been insured "that same morning, for slightly less than she was worth." Critics who reviewed the book found its prose ______ from first chapter to last.
worlds.explanation: Disasters get the same tone as seed prices, and the funniest details are passed over as quickly as anything else, so the humor comes from an unchanged, expressionless delivery: the prose is "deadpan." "Didactic" fails because he moves on from each event without drawing anything from it. "Digressive" fails because the chapter moves from one event of the winter to the next. "Florid" fails because he describes catastrophe in the voice he uses for seed prices, the reverse of ornate.

didactic.quote: passed over as quickly as the rest
didactic.why: an author who hurries past every detail does not stop to draw lessons

digressive.quote: a barn fire, a hailstorm that killed his only cow
digressive.why: the chapter reports the winter's events in turn rather than wandering from them

florid.quote: the tone he uses elsewhere for the price of seed
florid.why: the language for disaster is as plain as a price list, not ornate

worlds.passage: In 1958 a retired wheat farmer published a memoir of his forty years on the plains, with a chapter for each season of the farm year. The chapter on planting winter wheat gives the wheat its first two pages and then ten more to a grandfather, a county road, and a neighbor's quarrel, each leading to the next, before the wheat returns in the final paragraph. Nearly every chapter follows that pattern, so a reader can lose track of which season the book has reached. Critics who reviewed the book found its prose ______ from first chapter to last.
worlds.explanation: A chapter on wheat gives its subject two pages, spends ten on a chain of other matters, and returns only at the end, and the pattern repeats until readers lose their place in the year: the prose is "digressive." "Didactic" fails because the chapters wander among stories rather than delivering lessons. "Deadpan" fails because the passage describes the prose's course, not a flat comic delivery. "Florid" fails because the problem is where the prose goes, not how ornate its wording is.

didactic.quote: a grandfather, a county road, and a neighbor's quarrel
didactic.why: the chapters drift into unrelated matters, not into instruction for the reader

deadpan.why: the effect described is confusion from wandering, not humor from flat delivery

florid.quote: before the wheat returns in the final paragraph
florid.why: the feature is a departure from and return to the subject, not ornamented language

worlds.passage: In 1958 a retired wheat farmer published a memoir of his forty years on the plains, with a chapter for each season of the farm year. In his pages a summer sunrise over the stubble is "a blaze of molten brass poured upon a tapestry of gold." Milking a cow, mending a fence, and hauling grain to market each get the same treatment, so that reviewers quoting the book had trouble finding a single sentence about a farm chore put simply. Critics who reviewed the book found its prose ______ from first chapter to last.
worlds.explanation: The brass-and-tapestry sunrise is typical, since every chore gets the same treatment and plain sentences are almost impossible to find, so the prose is "florid," excessively ornate. "Didactic" fails because the chores are decorated, not turned into lessons. "Deadpan" fails because the prose never states anything simply. "Digressive" fails because each description stays on its chore; the excess lies in the wording.

didactic.why: the chores are elaborately described, not used to teach the reader

deadpan.quote: had trouble finding a single sentence
deadpan.why: prose with almost no plain sentences is the opposite of flat, unadorned delivery

digressive.quote: Milking a cow, mending a fence, and hauling grain
digressive.why: the prose describes each chore itself rather than leaving it for unrelated topics

topic_tag: a railway town and a port city
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: By 1930, one regional planner observed, the town had in effect become the city's ______.

worlds.passage: A small town lies forty miles north of a large port city, on a railway line opened in 1890. In the 1910s the railway added an early train south to the city and an evening train back, and cut the fare for monthly ticket holders. The town's own mills and shops closed one by one as new houses spread over its old fields, and by the late 1920s its streets were nearly empty on weekdays from the 6:40 departure until the evening train pulled in. By 1930, one regional planner observed, the town had in effect become the city's ______.
worlds.explanation: Commuter trains and cheap monthly fares, local mills closing, houses spreading, and streets empty from the morning train to the evening one together show a town whose people worked in the city and came home to sleep: the city's "dormitory." "Granary" fails because its fields were built over. "Getaway" fails because the traffic was townspeople leaving each morning, not city people arriving for leisure. "Garrison" fails because no troops are involved.

granary.quote: new houses spread over its old fields
granary.why: farmland became housing, so the town no longer supplied the city with grain

getaway.quote: nearly empty on weekdays from the 6:40 departure
getaway.why: the town emptied as residents left each workday, not filled with visitors from the city

garrison.quote: cut the fare for monthly ticket holders
garrison.why: the town's residents were regular commuters, not soldiers stationed to defend the city

worlds.passage: A small town lies forty miles north of a large port city, on a railway line opened in 1890. As the city grew, its bakers and brewers came to depend on wheat and barley from the farms north of it. The town's population stayed near two thousand through the 1920s, almost all of them farm families and the clerks who weighed grain at the station, and each autumn the railway ran extra freight trains south that came back empty. By 1930, one regional planner observed, the town had in effect become the city's ______.
worlds.explanation: The city's bakers and brewers relied on northern grain, the town was made up of farm families and grain clerks at the station, and autumn freight went south full and came back empty, so the town had become the city's "granary." "Dormitory" fails because its people worked on the farms and at the station, not in the city. "Getaway" fails because nothing brought city people north for leisure. "Garrison" fails because the town held farmers, not troops.

dormitory.quote: farm families and the clerks who weighed grain
dormitory.why: the townspeople worked locally on the farms and at the station rather than commuting

getaway.quote: extra freight trains south that came back empty
getaway.why: the trains carried cargo to the city and nothing back, not city residents out for leisure

garrison.quote: its bakers and brewers came to depend
garrison.why: the town's tie to the city is supplying grain, not stationing soldiers

worlds.passage: A small town lies forty miles north of a large port city, on a railway line opened in 1890. In the 1910s the railway began running Sunday excursion trains from the city to the lake beside the town. Through the 1920s city families filled every carriage on summer weekends to swim, picnic, and walk the hills, taking the evening train home, while the town's year-round residents ran the boat rentals and tea rooms that served them. By 1930, one regional planner observed, the town had in effect become the city's ______.
worlds.explanation: City families rode excursion trains out on weekends for swimming and walks and went home the same evening, so the town had become the city's "getaway," its place of escape. "Dormitory" fails because the visitors did not sleep there and the residents worked in the town serving them. "Granary" fails because the town's trade was leisure, not grain. "Garrison" fails because the visitors were families on outings, not soldiers.

dormitory.why: city visitors returned to sleep in the city, and the residents worked locally

granary.quote: ran the boat rentals and tea rooms
granary.why: the town lived on serving visitors, not on supplying the city with grain

garrison.quote: to swim, picnic, and walk the hills
garrison.why: the people arriving came for recreation, not to be stationed in defense of the city

worlds.passage: A small town lies forty miles north of a large port city, on a railway line opened in 1890. After a naval raid on the port in 1914, the army chose the town's station as the place from which troops could reach the city's docks within an hour. Through the 1920s three regiments took turns there, drilling all day on the old fairground and going to the city only for alerts and exercises, and the town's shops lived largely on the soldiers' pay. By 1930, one regional planner observed, the town had in effect become the city's ______.
worlds.explanation: The army placed regiments at the town so they could reach the port's docks within an hour, and they trained there and went to the city only when called, so the town had become the city's "garrison," the base of the force that defended it. "Dormitory" fails because the soldiers spent their days in the town and went to the city only on alert, rather than working there daily. "Getaway" fails because those arriving were stationed troops, not city people seeking leisure. "Granary" fails because the town lived on the soldiers' pay, not on grain.

dormitory.quote: drilling all day on the old fairground
dormitory.why: the soldiers spent their days in the town, so it was not where city workers merely slept

getaway.quote: After a naval raid on the port
getaway.why: the town's role grew out of defending the city, not out of city residents' leisure

granary.quote: lived largely on the soldiers' pay
granary.why: the town's economy depended on the troops, not on grain sent to the city

topic_tag: a village boatyard's role on its coast
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: Looking back on its first fifty years, one historian argued that the yard had served the coast above all as its ______.

worlds.passage: In 1871 the fishermen of a small harbor village on a rocky coast pooled their savings to open a boatyard. From its first keel, the yard wrote down each hull's timber, builder, and buyer, and added every later repair, sale, and change of name. Families quarreling over a boat, and buyers judging a secondhand hull, walked to the yard to look it up. By 1921 old fishermen up and down the coast were sending their grandsons there to learn which boats their own fathers had sailed. Looking back on its first fifty years, one historian argued that the yard had served the coast above all as its ______.
worlds.explanation: The yard kept each boat's whole history, and the coast came to it to recall that history, even across generations, so it served as the coast's "memory." "Lender" fails because people came to the yard to consult records, not to borrow; "insurer" fails because nothing is said about covering anyone's losses; "incubator" fails because nothing new grows out of the yard and leaves it: the grandsons come to learn the past, not a trade.

lender.quote: walked to the yard to look it up
lender.why: what people came to the yard for was information about a hull's past, not money or credit

insurer.quote: repair, sale, and change of name
insurer.why: the yard records what happened to each hull; nothing says it paid for any loss

incubator.quote: which boats their own fathers had sailed
incubator.why: the grandsons come to recover family history, not to be trained and sent out to found something new

worlds.passage: In 1871 the fishermen of a small harbor village on a rocky coast pooled their savings to open a boatyard. Few fishermen there had cash, and the nearest bank lay two days inland. A buyer could launch his boat at once and hand the yard a fifth of every season's catch. The yard's accounts show those shares stopping in the season the hull's price had been reached, often eight or ten years after its launch, and by 1921 most boats on that coast had been launched this way. Looking back on its first fifty years, one historian argued that the yard had served the coast above all as its ______.
worlds.explanation: Fishermen without cash took their boats at once and paid the yard from their catch only until each hull's price was covered, so the yard was acting as the coast's "lender." "Memory" fails because the accounts are the yard's own record of what it was owed, not a store of the coast's past that others consulted; "insurer" fails because the shares repaid a boat's price and covered no losses; "incubator" fails because the yard sold boats on credit and did not raise up new enterprises that went off on their own.

memory.quote: the season the hull's price had been reached
memory.why: the accounts track a debt until it is paid off; nothing is kept for the coast to remember

insurer.quote: a fifth of every season's catch
insurer.why: the shares pay for the buyer's own boat over time; no loss is being covered

incubator.quote: most boats on that coast had been launched this way
incubator.why: what spread along the coast was boats bought on credit, not enterprises that began at the yard and left it

worlds.passage: In 1871 the fishermen of a small harbor village on a rocky coast pooled their savings to open a boatyard. Every hull it sold cost a little more than its timber and labor, and the yard kept the difference apart from its own profits. After the storm of 1893 sank fourteen boats, it paid for fourteen new hulls, each handed at no charge to a family that had lost one, and by 1921 every boat lost on that coast had been rebuilt this way. Looking back on its first fifty years, one historian argued that the yard had served the coast above all as its ______.
worlds.explanation: Every buyer paid a little extra into a sum the yard kept apart, and that sum rebuilt the boats of whoever suffered a loss, so the yard served as the coast's "insurer." "Lender" fails because the new hulls were handed over at no charge and were never repaid; "memory" fails because the passage describes money held against losses, not a record of the coast's past; "incubator" fails because the yard restored existing fishing families rather than raising up new enterprises that went off on their own.

lender.why: the replacement hulls are not advanced to be repaid, so nothing is lent

memory.quote: kept the difference apart from its own profits
memory.why: what the yard held for the coast was money against losses, not a record of its past

incubator.quote: a family that had lost one
incubator.why: the fund restores what existing families lost; it starts no new enterprises

worlds.passage: In 1871 the fishermen of a small harbor village on a rocky coast pooled their savings to open a boatyard. Each year it took on two of the village's boys as apprentices, and after five years it let them go, since its own orders never grew. Most carried their tools to other harbors along that coast and built boats of their own. A survey of 1921 counted eleven yards on that coast, nine of them run by men born in the village. Looking back on its first fifty years, one historian argued that the yard had served the coast above all as its ______.
worlds.explanation: The yard trained boys, released them, and they founded most of the coast's other yards, so it served as the coast's "incubator." "Lender" fails because what the yard gave its apprentices was training, not money for their new yards; "insurer" fails because nothing is said about covering anyone's losses; "memory" fails because the yard's importance lies in the yards that grew from it, not in any record of the past it kept.

lender.quote: carried their tools to other harbors
lender.why: the apprentices took skills and tools from the yard, not credit; nothing is lent

insurer.quote: since its own orders never grew
insurer.why: the mechanism is a small yard training and releasing builders; no losses are covered

memory.quote: nine of them run by men born in the village
memory.why: the yard's legacy is the new yards its trainees founded, not a store of records

topic_tag: a mining valley's weekly newspaper
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: Writing a century later, one historian called the weekly the miners' ______.

worlds.passage: From 1884 to 1910 a mining valley's only newspaper was a four-page weekly sold at the pithead for a penny. Each issue printed a lesson in arithmetic, bookkeeping, or letter writing, and a miner who mailed in the exercises had them corrected and returned the following week. Mine records show that men who finished the full course were made weighmen, clerks, and foremen far more often than other miners, and several of their sons went on to the state university. Writing a century later, one historian called the weekly the miners' ______.
worlds.explanation: The weekly's lessons let miners qualify for better posts and their sons rise further, so it served as the miners' "ladder." "Jury" fails because the weekly corrected exercises and settled no disputes; "lens" fails because the lessons taught skills, not a way of interpreting events; "megaphone" fails because nothing the miners sent in was carried to any wider audience: their work came back to them corrected.

jury.why: the paper checks lessons; it is not weighing two sides of any dispute

lens.quote: were made weighmen, clerks, and foremen
lens.why: the effect of the weekly is promotion through skills, not a changed view of the world

megaphone.why: what miners sent the paper went back to them, not out to a larger audience

worlds.passage: From 1884 to 1910 a mining valley's only newspaper was a four-page weekly sold at the pithead for a penny. A miner who believed a foreman had cheated him on the weight of his coal could bring the matter to the paper, whose editor heard the miner and the foreman together and printed in the next issue a short finding that went against the miner about as often as for him. By the 1890s both the miners and the company usually accepted the paper's finding as final, and the valley's courts heard almost none of these disputes. Writing a century later, one historian called the weekly the miners' ______.
worlds.explanation: The weekly heard both sides of a dispute and issued a finding that both parties accepted, so it acted as the miners' "jury." "Megaphone" fails because the paper printed not the miners' complaints but its own ruling, which went against them about as often as for them; "lens" fails because the paper settled particular disputes rather than shaping how miners saw events; "ladder" fails because nothing helped miners rise to better positions.

megaphone.quote: heard the miner and the foreman together
megaphone.why: the paper hears both sides and prints only its own ruling, often against the miner, so it is not carrying the miners' voice to anyone

lens.quote: accepted the paper's finding as final
lens.why: the paper's role is deciding disputes, not providing a way of seeing the world

ladder.quote: courts heard almost none of these disputes
ladder.why: the paper's effect is on how disputes are settled, not on miners' advancement

worlds.passage: From 1884 to 1910 a mining valley's only newspaper was a four-page weekly sold at the pithead for a penny. For most miners it was the only news they saw, and each issue printed reports of distant strikes, tariffs, and elections, each followed by a column explaining what it would mean for men working underground. Diaries and union minutes from the valley in those years discuss faraway events almost always in that column's own terms and examples. worlds.passage: In 1790 a port-town printer sold a ballad about a young sailor who deserts his ship and drowns in a storm on his way home. A century later, folklorists collected it from singers who had learned it by ear. In nearly every version the topsail is now "the top of the hill," the home port is a name found on no map, and the sailor "weighs the anchor" by setting it on a scale. Asked what such lines meant, the singers shrugged and sang them again. Comparing the versions, one folklorist concluded that a hundred years of singing had ______ the ballad.
worlds.explanation: Words passed on by ear had turned into misheard phrases that no singer could explain, so singing had "mangled" the ballad. "Merged" fails because nothing from another song was joined to it; "mellowed" fails because the story is not softened, only garbled; "moralized" fails because the singers could not say what the lines meant, let alone draw a lesson from them.

merged.quote: a name found on no map
merged.why: the strange words come from mishearing, not from another song

mellowed.quote: by setting it on a scale
mellowed.why: the change is a garbled sense, not a gentler story

moralized.quote: the singers shrugged and sang them again
moralized.why: a lesson requires meaning, and the singers could not supply one
